promptLatex: Three tenths of the people in a town are left-handed. A test identifies a person's handedness correctly with probability 0.9 if the person is left-handed and with probability 0.2 if the person is right-handed. A person reports that the test says they are left-handed. What is the probability that the person really is left-handed?
hintLatex: Take a large population and count how many left-handed and how many right-handed people the test calls left-handed.
Out of $1000$ people, $300$ are left-handed and $700$ are right-handed; the test calls $270$ and $140$ of them respectively left-handed.
So $410$ people are called left-handed and $270$ of them really are.
solutionLatex:
Take a population of $1000$ people. Of these, $300$ are left-handed and $700$ are right-handed.

The test calls $0.9 \cdot 300 = 270$ of the left-handed people left-handed, and $0.2 \cdot 700 = 140$ of the right-handed people left-handed.

Altogether $270 + 140 = 410$ people are reported left-handed, of whom $270$ really are.

P(L \mid +) = \frac{270}{410} = \frac{27}{41}
